blocks.text: The name ἀνόπαια [anopaia] could also have been derived from אנפה anapha; Homer uses it for a species of eagle when he says of Minerva, Odyss. ά. line 320:
Ὄρνις δ᾽ ὡς ἀνόπαια διέπτατο, [Ornis d' hōs anopaia dieptato,]

Like an anopaea bird she flew away. On this passage Eustathius says: Ἀνόπαια, εἶδός τινες ὀρνέου λέγουσιν ἀετώδους Φήνῃ ἐοικότος· [Anopaia, eidos tines orneou legousin aetōdous Phēnē eoikotos;] Anopaea, as some report, is a species of bird of the eagle kind, similar to the ossifrage. Others hold that Minerva is compared [col. 338] [III, 100] with this bird διὰ τὸ ὡς ὄρνις ταχέως ὁρμῆσαι [dia to hōs ornis tacheōs hormēsai], because like a bird she rushes swiftly, as the old Scholiast has it. This would fit best if the bird ἀνόπαια [anopaia] were the same as אנפה anapha, or زمج [zummaj] zummag. For the Arabs say this is من خفاف الجوارح [min khifāf al-jawāriḥ] among the swiftest of birds of prey. Yet the bird زمج [zummaj] zummag does not seem to have been known to the Greeks, since its description occurs neither in Aristotle nor anywhere in other authors. But I would think that the Phoenicians who crossed into Greece with Cadmus called by the name אנפה anapha another bird similar to it, which was called in Greek ἀνόπαια [anopaia].

There is a kind of falcon which is called montanus [mountain falcon], by the barbarians montanarius, about which Albertus says: Its body is short and very thick, and the tail especially so. The breast is quite round and large; the legs are strong and short in proportion to the body; the feet knotty; the talons strong. It is accustomed to look at its feet frequently. On the back and the outside of the wings the colour is ash-grey, which gradually becomes ever clearer and paler the more often it has moulted, with a moderate dusky variegation interspersed. The name anapha would suit this falcon best, because no bird is more prone to anger, if we believe Albertus, whose words are: This kind of falcon is wild and endowed with bad habits, irascible, of inconstant anger. Thus a falconer who has sufficiently understood its habits is rare. He adds that it should seldom be held on the hand, except at dawn, at the time of hunting, and when it is to be fed. For thus it grows gentle toward the falconer's hand as toward a benefactor, and lays aside its anger. Likewise: When it is angry, let the falconer not resist it much, for thus its anger subsides more quickly. And again: If the prey escapes, it is indignant beyond all others, so that in its anger it sometimes attacks the one calling it back, and tears the head or face of the falconer, or of the horse on which he sits. He adds: There are times when one falcon attacks another; in this case a patient falconer is required, who does not oppose it, but patiently refrains from calling it back until, its anger laid aside, the falcon's spirit grows gentle. And shortly after: Having laid aside its anger, it will return of its own accord to the falconer's house. And further below: If it grows immoderately heated through anger, it hurls itself to its death, which some of our companions had already observed to have happened in the Alps. Likewise: When a mountain falcon, coming from a crag, was pursuing a partridge, and an eagle, chancing to fly up from the opposite side, had snatched it from it, and the falcon could not wrest it back from the eagle, after trying in vain for some time it at last mounted very high and, making a downward rush and striking the eagle's head, killed itself and the eagle alike. One must therefore always take care that it does not fall into so great a rage. It is more common than the other falcons, and delights wonderfully in its own ferocity. Thus falcons of this kind are often found for whom it is not enough to have wounded and brought down one bird, but who seem to glory in bringing down many. And sometimes they so indulge their cruelty that, busied with killing birds, they forget their food. So Albertus^{(1)} [III, 101] in Gesner, who hewed and smoothed what was crude in his language. From this description it appears that there is no bird, indeed no animal at all, more irascible than this falcon. But whether this bird was known long ago in the East is rightly doubted. Albertus indeed cites some things about this very bird from a king of Egypt, Ptolemy. It is a precept, he says, of Ptolemy, king of Egypt, that it should seldom be held on the hand. Likewise: Ptolemy instructs the diligent falconer not to release this falcon too often against strong birds. But these precepts of Ptolemy are as clumsily fabricated as the Epistle, bandied about today, of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, on the various kinds of falcons and their diseases and [col. 339] remedies. Its very title amply refutes it: for Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion were neither contemporaries of one another nor of the Ptolemies, but lived one or two centuries later; nor did they devote themselves to the art of fowling, but to the study of letters and the translation of the Bible. What of the fact that we have already proved above ^{c)} that this art is much more recent? Yet they are made to cite writings of the ancients, as if the ancients had written on the art of fowling long before.
